title: Toponymic Capital: Cities as Status Labels in the Semiotic Economy of Residence, Origin, and Destination
content: Urban science has learned to measure cities through the flows that cross them: capital, labour, information, and air traffic. It has paid far less attention to what the name of a city does when a person speaks it about themselves. "I live in London", "I am flying in from Milan", and "I am going to Burlington" are not neutral statements of location; each converts a place into a public claim about the speaker's wealth, mobility, taste, and future. This study theorizes that conversion as toponymic capital: the convertible symbolic value that accrues to a person through the city names attached to their residence, origin, destination, and transit. Drawing on Bourdieusian field theory, Peircean and post-Silversteinian semiotics, mobilities research, and the postcolonial critique of world-city hierarchies, the study conducts a comparative interpretive semiotic analysis of 24 publicly documented instances spanning Africa, Europe, North America, Latin America, the Gulf, South Asia, and East Asia, sourced from vernacular lexicons, platform practices, popular culture, and institutional instruments. Four findings follow. City names operate through a positional grammar in which destination and transit outrank residence; their value is fixed by the audience's reference frame rather than by the city alone; their polarity reverses under identifiable conditions that enable toponymic arbitrage; and their value converts into marriage prospects, credit, employment, and visa access. The study presents a toponymic status grammar as a measurable construct and sets out its implications for city branding, urban rankings, and the study of spatial inequality.
